Dell fell 10% Friday afternoon to $281.12 with no company news as the AI selloff deepened. HPE was down 9%, Super Micro 7% and Nvidia 7%.

Dell Technologies (NYSE: DELL) fell 10% Friday afternoon to $281.12 as the selloff in AI and chip stocks deepened, two trading sessions before the company reports earnings on Tuesday. No company news came with the drop. Dell is down 34% in November, on pace for its worst month since it returned to the stock market in 2018.

Other makers of AI servers fell with it. Hewlett Packard Enterprise (NYSE: HPE) was down 9% and Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI) 7%. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), whose chips go into Dell's AI servers, was down 7%. Nvidia has closed lower six sessions in a row, and a lower close on Friday would be the seventh. Prices are from about 12:53 p.m. Eastern.

24/7 Wall St.

The drop reads as investors cutting their AI hardware holdings ahead of the report: no Dell news arrived on Friday, and its peers fell together. That reading has a limit. Dell's own numbers arrive Tuesday, and the stock has moved 13% on average the day after its last eight reports, more than Friday's drop.

title: What HPE Holders Should Watch In Monday's Margin
detail:
What HPE Holders Should Watch In Monday's Margin

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Hewlett Packard Enterprise reports its fiscal fourth quarter on Monday, Nov 23, after the market close. Can HPE's AI servers lift its margin, or only its sales? The short answer is mixed. So far, HPE's margin has risen along with its sales. But HPE credits ordinary servers and networking for that, not AI servers. HPE itself expects AI servers to pull the margin back down.

Gross margin is the share of sales left after the direct cost of making the products. HPE's gross margin was 40.1% in the three months to July. A year earlier it was 29.2%. Revenue grew 33.7% over the same year.

AI servers were a small part of that. HPE's AI Systems revenue was almost $1.6 billion in the quarter. That is less than 13.1% of its revenue. HPE said the margin came from "disciplined pricing in traditional servers and increased networking mix".

We expect most previews to focus on AI server orders. This article looks at one number instead, the gross margin.

Where does HPE stock stand before the report?

HPE closed at $45.49 on Thursday. That is 38.1% below its Oct 9 close of $73.46, its highest of the past year. On Thursday, the S&P 500 fell 2.02%. HPE slipped 0.63%.

HPE now sits 38.1% under its October high, and Monday's report can move it again. If HPE is a big part of your savings, that is a fall you may have to sit through. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record.

The other AI hardware names have fallen further from their peak closes of the past year:

Dell Technologies is 46.9% below its Sep 17 record close.

Super Micro Computer is 52.5% below its June 2 high.

Nvidia, which makes the chips inside these servers, is 39.0% below its Oct 6 record close.

Did HPE's margin rise because of AI servers?

Not by HPE's own account. Its gross margin bottomed at 28.4% in the quarter to April 2025. It then rose in each of the next five quarters, to 40.1%. That is the highest of the 11 quarters Morningstar returns.

It is also well above HPE's normal level. Its gross margin averaged 33.1% a year from fiscal 2021 to 2025.

The server unit grew, but on price, not AI. HPE's Cloud & AI unit had $9 billion of revenue. HPE said higher prices for ordinary servers drove server revenue to an all-time high. The unit's operating margin, the share of sales left after all running costs, was 17%.

What does HPE expect AI servers to do to its margin?

HPE expects the margin to come down. It said gross margin should "moderate toward more historical levels". It named two causes, growth in AI systems and ordinary server margins returning to normal. More networking should partly offset that.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) has been one of the most searched-for stocks on Zacks.com lately. So, you might want to look at some of the facts that could shape the stock's performance in the near term.

Over the past month, shares of this server technology company have returned -29.3%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -6.6% change. During this period, the Zacks Computer- Storage Devices industry, which Super Micro falls in, has lost 30.8%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Revisions to Earnings Estimates

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

Super Micro is expected to post earnings of $1.68 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +143.5%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed +88.7%.

The consensus earnings estimate of $6.34 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +74.7%. This estimate has changed +49.8% over the last 30 days.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $6.63 indicates a change of +4.6% from what Super Micro is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +29.1%.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. HPE to Gain From Rising Demand for AI Compute and Storage

Hewlett Packard Enterprise is gaining from the rising demand for enterprise inferencing, agentic AI and allied data-intensive workloads. The company's Cloud & AI revenues have shown double-digit growth for the past two years. The trend is likely to have continued in the to-be-reported quarter.

Nvidia's SEC Probe Isn't Going Away, Even as a Blowout Quarter and a CEO Shake-Up Steal the Spotlight ©sasha85ru from Getty Images, Jordan Harrison from Pexels
Key Takeaways

NVIDIA reported $115.8 billion of quarterly revenue, up 103%, as the Wall Street Journal reported an SEC civil probe into whether its disclosures misled investors.

The Financial Times reported that NVIDIA booked $104 billion, almost half its 2025 sales, through Singapore in the same year it stopped breaking out Singapore in its results.

NVIDIA's $96.7 billion of free cash flow says the sales are real, and Super Micro Computer, whose co-founder faces charges of routing NVIDIA-powered servers to China, has a stake in how far the scrutiny spreads.

At about 13x forward earnings, NVIDIA already trades at a steep discount, but the probe will likely hang over the stock until the SEC says what it found.

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) gave investors plenty to cheer on Nov. 17: $115.8 billion of revenue for its October quarter, up 103%, in its first report since Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO. But just before those numbers came out, the Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC has opened a civil probe into whether NVIDIA's disclosures misled investors.

Much of the scrutiny centers on sales that ran through Southeast Asia, the same region prosecutors say a co-founder of Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) used to send NVIDIA-powered servers to China.

What exactly happened

Singapore is the likeliest place for the SEC to look. The Financial Times reported on Nov. 17 that NVIDIA booked $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, almost half its global sales. That was also the year NVIDIA stopped breaking out Singapore, switching its geographic split from where customers are billed to where they're headquartered.

The last time NVIDIA broke out Singapore, on its August 2025 earnings call, CFO Colette Kress said: "Over 99% of Data Center compute revenue billed to Singapore was for US-based customers." Kress is now also NVIDIA's interim CEO, and she kept the CFO job when she took over.

Then there's Megaspeed, the Singapore company whose former CEO, Alice Huang, was named in reports of an affair with Jensen Huang before his resignation. Earlier this year, Indonesian police acting on an FBI request found server racks but no GPUs at a Megaspeed site, the Straits Times reported, citing an unnamed official. Indonesia's police chief confirmed the FBI request on Nov. 17 but denied that a search had taken place. In a Nov. 16 joint statement, Commerce and the Justice Department said NVIDIA put Megaspeed on its "no sell" list in June 2025, a month after Commerce investigators asked NVIDIA for records.

title: Short Seller Raises Questions About Nvidia's Former Top Sales Executive. $2.5 Billion China Chip Case In Focus.

Short Seller Raises Questions About Nvidia's Former Top Sales Executive. $2.5 Billion China Chip Case In Focus.

Nvidia's former top sales executive has been drawn into fresh questions surrounding an alleged $2.5 billion scheme to divert advanced American AI technology to China, after a short seller highlighted a possible personal connection between him and a former Super Micro Computer official mentioned in a shareholder lawsuit.

Ajay "Jay" Puri, who previously oversaw Nvidia's worldwide sales operations, appeared in photographs with a woman identified as Cenly Chen or Cenly Puri, according to a report published by Muddy Waters Research. The firm questioned whether she was the same Cenly Chen who served as Super Micro's chief growth officer and whose responsibilities have come under scrutiny in litigation involving alleged violations of U.S. export restrictions.

The report does not establish that the woman pictured with Puri is the former Super Micro executive or independently verify a marital relationship. Neither Puri nor Chen has been charged in the federal criminal case, and the allegations involving Chen in the shareholder lawsuit have not been proven.

The questions are significant because Puri was among Nvidia's most senior executives before stepping down from his position in June, while Super Micro is a major customer that uses Nvidia's advanced graphics processors in its AI servers.

The shareholder lawsuit filed against Super Micro in October contains allegations from former employees concerning Chen's role in obtaining and allocating Nvidia chips.

According to the complaint, a former Super Micro sales director alleged that Chen managed the company's acquisition of graphics processors from Nvidia and decided how the limited supply would be distributed among customers.

The former employee also alleged that Chen regularly discussed chip allocations with Super Micro Chief Executive Charles Liang and sought approval for decisions involving major customers.

Another former employee claimed there was no way Chen could have been unaware of the company's alleged improper sales activities.

Those accounts are allegations included in a civil complaint, not findings by a court or conclusions reached by federal prosecutors.

The lawsuit also cites a former employee's allegation that Chen requested the release of Nvidia chips bearing serial numbers associated with products allegedly diverted to China. That claim has not been independently established.

The litigation followed a criminal investigation disclosed in March, when the U.S. Justice Department announced charges against three individuals accused of conspiring to circumvent American export controls.

title: Who is Cenly Chen? Inside the Alleged Family Ties Between Nvidia, Supermicro, and Illicit GPU Sales

Who is Cenly Chen? Inside the Alleged Family Ties Between Nvidia, Supermicro, and Illicit GPU Sales

Nvidia (NVDA) faces a notable but underappreciated governance question after a Muddy Waters short seller report raised alarms that Jay Puri, the chipmaker's longtime worldwide sales chief and former third-ranking executive, is married to Cenly Chen, a former Super Micro Computer (SMCI) executive. Chen resigned earlier this year, about a month after US prosecutors charged three people tied to the server maker over an alleged $2.5 billion scheme to divert Nvidia-equipped servers to China.

Muddy Waters said it could not independently verify that the Chen photographed alongside Puri is the same woman employed by Super Micro. However, reporting by The Information and a shareholder lawsuit both appear to confirm her identity, with the civil complaint stating there was "no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge of SMCI's illicit sales."

That revelation puts a fresh spotlight on how Nvidia's most sought-after chips were allocated, and on whether the company's filings told investors the full story.

From Account Manager to Chief Growth Officer

Chen spent roughly 18 years at Supermicro, rising from account manager in 2008 through a series of sales leadership roles to become chief growth officer in October 2023, and she now serves as CEO of ChronoScale (CHRN), a Nasdaq-listed AI compute firm.

Super Micro co-founder Wally Liaw is among the three people charged in the alleged diversion scheme, while Chen herself has not been criminally charged.

Why the Puri-Chen Link Matters

The concern is structural rather than personal, because Puri reportedly controlled chip allocations to server partners, while a shareholder class action alleges that Chen decided how Nvidia racks were distributed among Super Micro customers, potentially placing both ends of the GPU pipeline within a single household.

The October complaint, drawing on former employees, alleges that Chen must have known about the illicit sales and that she suppressed internal discussion of company scandals.

It further alleges that she was pushed out after emailing Nvidia to release chips whose serial numbers were linked to diverted GPUs, a striking claim given how closely her exit followed the criminal charges.

title: Muddy Waters Has Issued a New Short Call on Nvidia. I Still Expect NVDA Stock to Grind Higher.
detail:
Muddy Waters Has Issued a New Short Call on Nvidia. I Still Expect NVDA Stock to Grind Higher.
Ebube Jones

Nvidia (NVDA) hit a record $243.37 on Oct. 6, then fell to a 52-week low of $148.80 on Nov. 12, the day Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, president, and a board member. The selloff erased roughly $1 trillion in market value in six trading sessions. CFO Colette Kress took over as interim CEO, and NVDA stock was still about 35% below its peak heading into earnings.

On Nov. 12, "The Big Short" investor Michael Burry said he'd doubled his put position against the Nasdaq-100 ($IUXX) and that he expects chip stocks to get cheaper. Then, hours before the Nov. 17 earnings report, Muddy Waters disclosed a short position on Nvidia. The short seller questioned whether a former Nvidia executive had ties to a Super Micro (SMCI) executive named in a lawsuit involving alleged chip diversion to China. The stock was already down about 2% that day, and short interest stood at 1.16%.

Yet in its Q3 earnings results, Nvidia went on to beat Wall Street's expectations, reporting $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% from a year earlier. But it broke with its usual practice by reporting earnings without filing its quarterly Form 10-Q at the same time. The filing wasn't overdue, but investors will have to wait for the fuller picture. So does Muddy Waters have a point, or do the latest results make NVDA stock harder to bet against? Let's find out.

Is Muddy Waters' Short Call on Nvidia Justified?

Muddy Waters is right to ask where Nvidia's chips actually end up, but the report doesn't make a strong case that the stock is overvalued. The report asks whether restricted chips are reaching China through server suppliers. It points to a federal indictment alleging that three people tied to Super Micro Computer helped divert about $2.5 billion worth of servers containing the chips to China.

If some sales booked outside China ultimately depend on Chinese buyers, tighter enforcement could hurt demand. But the $2.5 billion is the alleged value of the servers, not what the chipmaker earned or what it stands to lose.

The report is less convincing when it tries to tie Nvidia directly to the alleged diversion. It cites photos of former executive Ajay Puri with a woman it hadn't confirmed was Cenly Chen, who was named in a separate shareholder lawsuit. Super Micro Computer said Chen didn't manage the relationship with the chipmaker or decide where the chips went. Even if the woman was Chen, the photos wouldn't show that Nvidia knew about the alleged diversion.
